osces.title: Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis - Diagnosis and Treatment

patient_demographics.name: Rachel Thompson
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: worsening asthma with brown mucus plugs

osces.clinical_scenario: Ms Thompson presents to the respiratory clinic with a 6-month history of poorly controlled asthma despite high-dose ICS-LABA therapy. She reports coughing up brown, rubbery mucus plugs and experiencing recurrent chest infections. She has a history of moderate persistent asthma since childhood and allergic rhinitis. Recent chest X-ray shows fleeting upper lobe infiltrates.

presenting_complaint.main_symptom: worsening asthma control with expectoration of brown mucus plugs
presenting_complaint.character: thick, brown, rubbery sputum plugs, difficult to expectorate
presenting_complaint.exacerbating_factors: exposure to mould in classroom, humid weather
presenting_complaint.relieving_factors: temporary improvement with oral prednisolone courses
presenting_complaint.associated_symptoms: wheeze, dyspnoea, chest tightness, fatigue, weight loss of 3kg

medical_history: 3 hospital admissions for asthma in past year
history_taking.allergies: house dust mites, Aspergillus fumigatus (skin prick test positive), grass pollen

social_history.occupation: primary school teacher, old building with visible mould

history_taking.family_history: mother has asthma, father has eczema

physical_examination.general: young woman, mild respiratory distress, using accessory muscles, speaks in full sentences

respiratory.inspection: increased work of breathing, no cyanosis, no clubbing
respiratory.percussion: dull percussion note right upper zone
respiratory.auscultation: widespread polyphonic expiratory wheeze, coarse crackles right upper lobe

physical_examination.cardiovascular: dual heart sounds, no murmurs, no peripheral oedema
physical_examination.other: nasal polyps visible on anterior rhinoscopy

initial.result: FEV1 1.8L (52% predicted), FVC 3.1L (75% predicted), FEV1/FVC 58%, post-bronchodilator FEV1 2.2L (64% predicted) - 22% improvement
Hb 128 g/L, WCC 12.3 x10^9/L, eosinophils 2.8 x10^9/L (23%), platelets 342 x10^9/L
2,840 IU/mL (normal <100 IU/mL)
48.2 kUA/L (positive >0.35 kUA/L)
142 mg/L (positive >40 mg/L)
right upper lobe consolidation with mucoid impaction, central bronchiectasis, previous left upper lobe infiltrate now resolved
central bronchiectasis, mucoid impaction in dilated bronchi ('finger-in-glove' sign), mosaic attenuation, right upper lobe consolidation
Aspergillus fumigatus isolated, sensitive to itraconazole and voriconazole

diagnosis.diagnostic_criteria: meets ISHAM working group criteria: asthma, total IgE >1000 IU/mL, positive Aspergillus IgE and IgG, eosinophilia >500 cells/μL, radiological findings consistent with ABPA

pharmacological.dose: 0.5mg/kg/day (35mg) for 2 weeks, then taper over 3-6 months
pharmacological.monitoring: blood glucose, bone density if prolonged use
liver function tests monthly, drug levels, QTc monitoring

non_pharmacological: mould remediation at home and workplace
management.follow_up: respiratory clinic in 4 weeks with repeat IgE, eosinophil count, and chest X-ray

marking_criteria.criterion: identifies key features of ABPA presentation
appropriate history taking including occupational exposure
recognises significance of brown mucus plugs
orders appropriate investigations including Aspergillus serology
correctly interprets elevated IgE and eosinophilia
demonstrates safe prescribing with PBS authority requirements

osces.sample_answer: 28-year-old female teacher with poorly controlled asthma presenting with brown mucus plugs and recurrent infections. Examination reveals wheeze and right upper lobe crackles. Investigations show eosinophilia (2.8 x10^9/L), total IgE 2,840 IU/mL, positive Aspergillus IgE and IgG, and HRCT demonstrating central bronchiectasis with mucoid impaction. Diagnosis of ABPA confirmed using ISHAM criteria. Management includes prednisolone 35mg daily with gradual taper, itraconazole 200mg BD for 16 weeks (PBS authority 8470W), continued high-dose ICS-LABA, environmental mould remediation, and close monitoring of treatment response with serial IgE levels.

osces.title: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency - Diagnosis and Augmentation Therapy
osces.clinical_scenario: Mr O'Brien, a 42-year-old never-smoker, presents with a 3-year history of progressive exertional dyspnoea. He was recently diagnosed with emphysema on CT chest performed for unrelated reasons. He reports his younger brother was diagnosed with 'liver problems' at age 35. He has noticed increasing breathlessness affecting his work performance and has had two chest infections in the past 6 months requiring antibiotics.

presenting_complaint.character: breathlessness on moderate exertion, walking one flight of stairs
presenting_complaint.exacerbating_factors: physical activity, cold air, dust exposure at work
presenting_complaint.relieving_factors: rest, salbutamol inhaler provides minimal relief
presenting_complaint.associated_symptoms: chronic dry cough, fatigue, no wheeze, no sputum production

social_history.occupation: warehouse supervisor, dust exposure, some heavy lifting
social_history.exercise: previously played social soccer, stopped due to breathlessness

history_taking.family_history: brother diagnosed with cirrhosis age 35 (non-drinker), maternal grandfather died of 'lung disease' age 58, parents of Irish descent

physical_examination.general: well-appearing man, mild dyspnoea at rest, no distress

respiratory.inspection: increased AP diameter, mild use of accessory muscles
respiratory.auscultation: globally reduced breath sounds, no wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase

physical_examination.cardiovascular: normal heart sounds, no murmurs, no peripheral oedema
physical_examination.abdomen: soft, non-tender, liver palpable 1cm below costal margin, no splenomegaly

initial.result: FEV1 1.95L (48% predicted), FVC 4.2L (82% predicted), FEV1/FVC 46%, post-bronchodilator FEV1 2.05L (51% predicted) - minimal reversibility, DLCO 45% predicted
0.42 g/L (normal 0.9-2.0 g/L)
PiZZ phenotype confirmed
ALT 68 U/L (normal <40), AST 52 U/L (normal <40), GGT 45 U/L, bilirubin 18 μmol/L, albumin 38 g/L
panlobular emphysema with basal predominance, no bronchiectasis, no nodules
pH 7.41, PaO2 68 mmHg, PaCO2 38 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, SaO2 93%
hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, increased retrosternal airspace, paucity of vascular markings lower zones
mild hepatomegaly, increased echogenicity suggesting fatty infiltration, no cirrhosis

diagnosis.primary: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ phenotype) with emphysema
diagnosis.diagnostic_criteria: serum AAT level <0.5 g/L, PiZZ phenotype, panlobular emphysema with basal predominance in never-smoker

immediate: supplemental oxygen if SpO2 <88% on exertion
smoking cessation counselling for household members

pharmacological.pbs_code: not PBS listed - accessed via Life Saving Drugs Program
pharmacological.monitoring: trough AAT levels monthly initially, pulmonary function tests 6-monthly

non_pharmacological: avoid occupational dust exposure - consider work modification
family screening for siblings and children
management.follow_up: respiratory physician 3-monthly, hepatology review annually, consideration for lung transplant evaluation if FEV1 <30% predicted

marking_criteria.criterion: recognises early-onset emphysema in never-smoker as red flag
takes appropriate family history including liver disease
orders alpha-1 antitrypsin level and phenotyping
screens for liver involvement with LFTs and imaging
discusses augmentation therapy with IV alpha-1 proteinase inhibitor
aware of Life Saving Drugs Program for access in Australia
discusses lung transplant criteria and timing

osces.sample_answer: 42-year-old never-smoker with progressive dyspnoea and early-onset emphysema. Family history significant for brother with cirrhosis. Examination shows hyperinflation with reduced breath sounds. Spirometry confirms severe fixed airflow obstruction (FEV1 48% predicted). Alpha-1 antitrypsin level 0.42 g/L with PiZZ phenotype confirms diagnosis. HRCT shows basilar-predominant panlobular emphysema. Mild liver involvement with elevated transaminases. Management includes augmentation therapy with IV alpha-1 proteinase inhibitor 60mg/kg weekly (accessed via Life Saving Drugs Program), optimised bronchodilator therapy with tiotropium and ICS-LABA, pulmonary rehabilitation, family screening, genetic counselling, and regular monitoring. Consider transplant evaluation if disease progresses.

osces.title: Pulmonary Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis - Smoking Cessation

patient_demographics.name: Sophie Chen
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: dry cough and exertional dyspnoea with abnormal chest imaging

osces.clinical_scenario: Ms Chen presents following an abnormal chest X-ray performed for insurance purposes. She reports a 6-month history of dry cough and mild exertional dyspnoea. She is a current smoker (15 pack-years) and has noticed she gets more breathless than her colleagues when climbing stairs at work. HRCT shows multiple irregular cysts predominantly in the upper and mid zones with nodules. She has no systemic symptoms and specifically denies bone pain or polyuria.

presenting_complaint.main_symptom: dry cough with mild exertional dyspnoea
presenting_complaint.relieving_factors: rest, reduced smoking on weekends improves symptoms
presenting_complaint.associated_symptoms: no haemoptysis, no chest pain, no weight loss, no fever

social_history.smoking: 15 cigarettes daily for 12 years (15 pack-years), two previous quit attempts
social_history.occupation: marketing executive, office-based, frequent client dinners

history_taking.family_history: no lung disease, mother has osteoporosis, father has hypertension

physical_examination.general: well-appearing woman, no respiratory distress at rest, nicotine staining on fingers

respiratory.auscultation: vesicular breath sounds, no crackles or wheeze

initial.result: multiple irregular thin-walled cysts 2-20mm diameter, upper and mid zone predominance, sparing costophrenic angles, scattered nodules 3-5mm, no lymphadenopathy
FEV1 2.8L (85% predicted), FVC 3.4L (88% predicted), FEV1/FVC 82%, DLCO 68% predicted
Hb 138 g/L, WCC 8.2 x10^9/L, platelets 289 x10^9/L, normal differential
12 mm/hr (normal <20)
CD1a and Langerin positive cells, S100 positive, negative for BRAF V600E mutation
no lytic lesions
580 mOsm/kg (normal, no diabetes insipidus)
reticulonodular opacities upper zones, preserved lung volumes, no pneumothorax

diagnosis.diagnostic_criteria: typical HRCT findings with cysts and nodules, upper zone predominance, CD1a/Langerin positive on biopsy, current smoker

pharmacological.dose: 0.5mg daily for 3 days, then 0.5mg BD for 4 days, then 1mg BD for 11 weeks
21mg/24hr patch for 6 weeks, then 14mg for 2 weeks, then 7mg for 2 weeks

non_pharmacological: cognitive behavioural therapy for smoking cessation
avoid hormonal therapy (may worsen cystic lesions)
management.follow_up: respiratory clinic 3-monthly with PFTs and chest X-ray, HRCT annually, immediate review if pneumothorax symptoms

marking_criteria.criterion: identifies smoking as primary aetiological factor
recognises typical HRCT pattern of PLCH
orders appropriate diagnostic tests including transbronchial biopsy
screens for systemic involvement (bones, diabetes insipidus)
prioritises smoking cessation as primary treatment
aware of PBS authority requirements for smoking cessation
advises against air travel until stable

osces.sample_answer: 34-year-old female smoker (15 pack-years) with 6-month history of dry cough and exertional dyspnoea. HRCT shows characteristic upper zone predominant cystic and nodular changes. Transbronchial biopsy confirms PLCH with CD1a/Langerin positive staining. DLCO mildly reduced at 68% predicted. No systemic involvement on screening. Primary treatment is smoking cessation - prescribed varenicline 1mg BD (PBS 8976F) with nicotine replacement therapy, Quitline referral (13 78 48), and behavioural support. Counselled about 25% pneumothorax risk, advised against air travel until stable, and to avoid hormonal therapy. Follow-up 3-monthly with PFTs to monitor response to smoking cessation. Prognosis good if achieves sustained smoking cessation.

osces.title: Massive Haemoptysis - Emergency Management and Bronchial Artery Embolization

patient_demographics.name: Dimitri Papadopoulos
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: coughing up large amounts of blood

osces.clinical_scenario: Mr Papadopoulos presents to the emergency department after coughing up approximately 300mL of bright red blood over the past 2 hours. He has a history of bronchiectasis secondary to childhood measles and recurrent infections. He reports increasing sputum production over the past week with fever and has been on oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for 3 days. He suddenly developed massive haemoptysis while watching television. He is anxious, coughing frequently, and has visible blood around his mouth.

presenting_complaint.volume: estimated 300mL total, bright red, with clots
presenting_complaint.trigger: coughing fit after feeling 'gurgling' in chest
presenting_complaint.associated_symptoms: dyspnoea, anxiety, chest discomfort right lower zone, dizziness

medications: amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125mg BD (day 3 of course) - PBS code 2089T
previously on azithromycin prophylaxis (stopped 6 months ago)

social_history.smoking: ex-smoker, quit 10 years ago, 30 pack-year history
social_history.occupation: retired construction worker, asbestos exposure in 1980s
social_history.travel: born in Greece, migrated 1975, recent travel to Greece 3 months ago

history_taking.family_history: no bleeding disorders, no lung disease

physical_examination.general: anxious man, fresh blood around mouth, pale, coughing intermittently producing blood

respiratory.inspection: blood-stained tissues, tachypnoeic, using accessory muscles
respiratory.auscultation: coarse crackles right lower and middle zones, scattered crackles left base, no wheeze

physical_examination.cardiovascular: tachycardic, normal heart sounds, cool peripheries, CRT 3 seconds
physical_examination.ent: fresh blood in oropharynx, no active bleeding site visible

initial.result: Hb 98 g/L (was 135 g/L 3 months ago), WCC 16.8 x10^9/L, platelets 423 x10^9/L
PT 13.2 sec, APTT 32 sec, INR 1.1, fibrinogen 4.8 g/L - all normal
O positive, antibody screen negative, 4 units packed red cells crossmatched
pH 7.46, PaO2 58 mmHg, PaCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3 23 mmol/L, lactate 2.8 mmol/L
right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, bronchiectatic changes bilaterally, no mass
extensive bronchiectasis right middle and lower lobes, active contrast extravasation from hypertrophied right bronchial artery, consolidation right lower lobe
pending (sent prior to antibiotics: later grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa)

diagnosis.primary: massive haemoptysis secondary to infected bronchiectasis with bronchial artery bleeding
diagnosis.diagnostic_criteria: volume >100mL/24hr, haemodynamic compromise, CT evidence of active bleeding from bronchial artery

immediate: position patient right side down (bleeding lung dependent)
high flow oxygen 15L/min via non-rebreather mask
fluid resuscitation with normal saline 1L stat
activate massive transfusion protocol if needed

pharmacological.dose: 1g IV over 10 minutes, then 1g over 8 hours

interventional: selective catheterisation of right bronchial artery
avoid spinal artery (anterior spinal from bronchial in 5%)
rigid bronchoscopy on standby for airway protection
management.follow_up: ICU monitoring 24-48 hours, daily chest X-ray, bronchoscopy once stable to exclude malignancy, long-term azithromycin prophylaxis

marking_criteria.criterion: recognises life-threatening nature requiring immediate action
positions patient with bleeding lung dependent
establishes adequate IV access and resuscitation
orders appropriate imaging including CT angiography
identifies bronchial artery as bleeding source
aware of bronchial artery embolization as definitive treatment
provides appropriate antibiotic cover for Pseudomonas
considers need for definitive surgery if embolization fails

osces.sample_answer: 58-year-old man with bronchiectasis presenting with massive haemoptysis (300mL in 2 hours), hypotension, and respiratory distress. Examination reveals right lower zone crackles with evidence of active bleeding. Immediate management: position right side down, high-flow oxygen, large-bore IV access x2, fluid resuscitation, tranexamic acid 1g IV stat. CT chest confirms active bleeding from right bronchial artery. Urgent interventional radiology for bronchial artery embolization performed successfully. Anti-pseudomonal antibiotics (ceftazidime 2g IV 8-hourly plus tobramycin). ICU admission for monitoring. Follow-up bronchoscopy once stable to exclude malignancy. Long-term management includes azithromycin prophylaxis and regular chest physiotherapy.

osces.title: Pneumomediastinum - Recognition and Conservative Management

patient_demographics.name: Jackson Williams
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: chest pain and neck swelling after vomiting

osces.clinical_scenario: Mr Williams, a 19-year-old university student, presents to the emergency department with sudden onset chest pain and neck discomfort. He reports attending a party last night where he consumed excessive alcohol and had multiple episodes of forceful vomiting. This morning he noticed his voice sounded different and his neck felt 'puffy'. He has sharp central chest pain worse with deep breathing and swallowing. He denies any trauma, recent air travel, or recreational drug use including marijuana.

presenting_complaint.main_symptom: central chest pain with neck swelling
presenting_complaint.associated_symptoms: voice change (higher pitched), neck discomfort, mild dysphagia, no dyspnoea at rest

medical_history: mild asthma in childhood (no medications currently)
medications: took ibuprofen 400mg this morning for pain

social_history.alcohol: social drinking, binge drinking 1-2 times per month
social_history.drugs: denies illicit drug use including marijuana
social_history.recent_activities: no scuba diving, no air travel, no heavy lifting, exam period stress

history_taking.family_history: no lung disease, no Marfan syndrome

physical_examination.general: anxious young man, speaking in short sentences due to pain, no respiratory distress

neck.inspection: visible swelling of neck and supraclavicular regions
neck.palpation: subcutaneous emphysema from jaw to clavicles, crepitus on palpation

respiratory.palpation: subcutaneous emphysema upper chest wall, equal expansion
respiratory.auscultation: vesicular breath sounds bilaterally, no wheeze or crackles, possible Hamman's sign (crunching sound with heartbeat)

physical_examination.cardiovascular: heart sounds normal but obscured by Hamman's sign, no murmurs
physical_examination.other: no signs of Marfan syndrome (normal arm span, no high arched palate)

initial.result: continuous diaphragm sign, pneumomediastinum with linear lucencies along cardiac borders, subcutaneous emphysema neck and chest wall, no pneumothorax, normal cardiac size
extensive pneumomediastinum tracking along bronchovascular bundles, subcutaneous emphysema, no pneumothorax, no oesophageal thickening, no underlying lung pathology
sinus rhythm 88 bpm, normal intervals, no ST changes, normal QRS voltage
Hb 148 g/L, WCC 9.2 x10^9/L with normal differential, platelets 267 x10^9/L
8 mg/L (normal <10)
no oesophageal perforation, normal oesophageal contour and mucosa
pH 7.42, PaO2 92 mmHg, PaCO2 38 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L (normal)

diagnosis.primary: spontaneous pneumomediastinum (Hamman syndrome) secondary to forceful vomiting
diagnosis.diagnostic_criteria: subcutaneous emphysema, radiological evidence of pneumomediastinum, absence of pneumothorax or oesophageal perforation, Hamman's sign present

non_pharmacological: high flow oxygen if subcutaneous emphysema extensive (aids reabsorption)
education about warning signs (increasing dyspnoea, chest pain)
management.follow_up: discharge after 24 hours observation if stable, chest X-ray in 1 week, respiratory clinic if not resolved in 2 weeks, immediate return if worsening symptoms

marking_criteria.criterion: recognises Hamman's sign (crunching sound) on examination
orders appropriate imaging (chest X-ray and CT)
recognises continuous diaphragm sign on X-ray
excludes oesophageal perforation with contrast study
understands benign nature requiring conservative management

osces.sample_answer: 19-year-old male presenting with chest pain and neck swelling after forceful vomiting. Examination reveals subcutaneous emphysema and Hamman's sign (crunching with heartbeat). Chest X-ray shows pneumomediastinum with continuous diaphragm sign, confirmed on CT. Water-soluble contrast swallow excludes oesophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndrome). Diagnosis is spontaneous pneumomediastinum (Hamman syndrome). Management is conservative with analgesia (paracetamol 1g QID, oxycodone PRN), antiemetics, 24-hour observation, and avoidance of Valsalva manoeuvres. Advised no air travel for 2 weeks. Follow-up chest X-ray in 1 week. Prognosis excellent with spontaneous resolution expected within 1-2 weeks.

osces.title: Tracheostomy Care - Tube Change and Emergency Management
osces.clinical_scenario: Mrs Robertson presents to the emergency department with acute respiratory distress. She has a tracheostomy inserted 3 months ago following prolonged intubation for Guillain-Barré syndrome. Her daughter reports that the tracheostomy tube appears blocked and suctioning at home has not helped. Mrs Robertson is using accessory muscles, appears distressed, and is unable to speak clearly through her speaking valve. Her regular tracheostomy change was due last week but was postponed due to a family emergency.

presenting_complaint.character: unable to pass suction catheter, increased work of breathing
presenting_complaint.attempted_interventions: home suctioning unsuccessful, removed speaking valve, increased oxygen
presenting_complaint.associated_symptoms: audible wheeze from stoma, minimal air movement, anxiety, unable to cough effectively

tracheostomy_details.home_care: family trained in suctioning and basic care

medications: gabapentin 300mg TDS for neuropathic pain - PBS code 8098H
regular saline nebulisers for secretion management

social_history.living: home with husband, daughter visits daily
social_history.home_equipment: suction machine, pulse oximeter, emergency bag

physical_examination.general: elderly woman in respiratory distress, using accessory muscles, diaphoretic

airway.tracheostomy_site: Shiley size 8 in situ, minimal air movement through tube, unable to pass size 12 suction catheter
airway.stoma: mild erythema around stoma, no purulent discharge, mature tract
airway.neck: no subcutaneous emphysema, no tracheal deviation

respiratory.auscultation: minimal air entry bilaterally, transmitted upper airway sounds

physical_examination.neurological: alert, follows commands, residual mild lower limb weakness

initial.result: pH 7.32, PaO2 55 mmHg, PaCO2 52 mmHg, HCO3 26 mmol/L, lactate 2.2 mmol/L
tracheostomy tube in good position, no pneumothorax, mild bibasal atelectasis
performed after stabilisation: normal supraglottic structures, vocal cords mobile, no granulation tissue

diagnosis.primary: blocked tracheostomy tube with mucus plug causing acute respiratory distress

immediate: attempt to pass suction catheter with saline lavage
if unsuccessful, immediate tracheostomy tube change
equipment ready: same size and one size smaller tubes, obturator, ties, lubricant
prepare for potential surgical airway if tract lost
emergency_tube_change_procedure: position patient semi-recumbent with neck extended
assistant to provide cricoid pressure if needed
remove old tube following curve while assistant maintains stoma patency
insert new lubricated tube with obturator following curve
confirm placement with ETCO2, bilateral air entry, patient comfort
post_procedure_care: inner cannula cleaning if double-lumen tube
education: family education on emergency tube change
provide emergency box with spare tubes
link with hospital in the home service
management.follow_up: ENT review in 1 week, consider fenestrated tube for speaking valve use, respiratory clinic 4-weekly, physiotherapy for secretion management

marking_criteria.criterion: prepares correct equipment for tube change
provides family education on emergency management

osces.sample_answer: 68-year-old woman with tracheostomy presenting with acute airway obstruction from blocked tube. Examination shows respiratory distress with SpO2 88% and inability to pass suction catheter. Immediate management: high-flow oxygen, attempted suction with saline lavage unsuccessful, proceeded to emergency tube change. Positioned patient, deflated cuff, removed blocked tube revealing thick mucus plug, inserted new Shiley size 8 tube smoothly, confirmed placement with ETCO2 and auscultation. Post-procedure: CXR confirmed position, commenced nebulised saline QID and acetylcysteine BD for secretion management. Family educated on emergency procedures, provided spare tubes and emergency plan. Arranged ENT follow-up and regular monthly changes through hospital-in-home service.
